abstract: BACKGROUND: Although several therapeutic agents have been evaluated for the treatment of coronavirus disease 2019 (Covid-19), no antiviral agents have yet been shown to be efficacious. METHODS: We conducted a double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial of intravenous remdesivir in adults who were hospitalized with Covid-19 and had evidence of lower respiratory tract infection. Patients were randomly assigned to receive either remdesivir (200 mg loading dose on day 1, followed by 100 mg daily for up to 9 additional days) or placebo for up to 10 days. The primary outcome was the time to recovery, defined by either discharge from the hospital or hospitalization for infection-control purposes only. RESULTS: A total of 1062 patients underwent randomization (with 541 assigned to remdesivir and 521 to placebo). Those who received remdesivir had a median recovery time of 10 days (95% confidence interval [CI], 9 to 11), as compared with 15 days (95% CI, 13 to 18) among those who received placebo (rate ratio for recovery, 1.29; 95% CI, 1.12 to 1.49; P<0.001, by a log-rank test). In an analysis that used a proportional-odds model with an eight-category ordinal scale, the patients who received remdesivir were found to be more likely than those who received placebo to have clinical improvement at day 15 (odds ratio, 1.5; 95% CI, 1.2 to 1.9, after adjustment for actual disease severity). The Kaplan-Meier estimates of mortality were 6.7% with remdesivir and 11.9% with placebo by day 15 and 11.4% with remdesivir and 15.2% with placebo by day 29 (hazard ratio, 0.73; 95% CI, 0.52 to 1.03). Serious adverse events were reported in 131 of the 532 patients who received remdesivir (24.6%) and in 163 of the 516 patients who received placebo (31.6%). CONCLUSIONS: Our data show that remdesivir was superior to placebo in shortening the time to recovery in adults who were hospitalized with Covid-19 and had evidence of lower respiratory tract infection. (Funded by the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases and others; ACTT-1 ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT04280705.).

narrative:
Short impact summary

This 2020 New England Journal of Medicine trial has become a major reference point in COVID-19 therapeutics, with 7,760 citations and placement in the top 1% most-cited papers for its field and year. Its influence is visible not only in scholarly uptake but also in teaching and broader scientific discussion, including four recorded YouTube uses, two Bluesky mentions, and active post-publication scrutiny.

Full narrative

“Remdesivir for the Treatment of Covid-19 — Final Report” is an early, high-profile randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of intravenous remdesivir in hospitalized adults with COVID-19 and lower respiratory tract infection. Published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2020, it quickly became one of the field’s core clinical trial reports, and its citation record shows sustained academic uptake across a broad international literature.

The paper’s citation performance is exceptional: 7,760 OpenAlex citations and a field- and year-normalized standing in the top 1% indicate that it is not merely visible but deeply embedded in the research conversation. The citing landscape is heavily concentrated in COVID-19 clinical research and SARS-CoV-2 studies, with substantial reuse in articles, preprints, reviews, and book chapters. Recent citing works also show continued relevance beyond the pandemic’s first phase, including later therapeutic reviews and methodologically related antiviral studies.

Attention outside conventional journal citations is present but comparatively modest. The record shows two online mentions on Bluesky, and the work appears in teaching-oriented video content, suggesting that it has served as an explanatory anchor for clinicians and educators discussing remdesivir and COVID-19 treatment. At the same time, the article has also attracted post-publication scrutiny, with three PubPeer threads and scite signals that are predominantly mentioning or supporting, alongside some contradicting statements, consistent with an active but not one-sided scientific debate.

The funding and stewardship record fits the scale of the study: it was supported through National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases and related United States funding streams, and it is linked to a registered clinical trial. Overall, the evidence portrays a paper that became central to the evidence base for COVID-19 antiviral therapy, was rapidly taken up across multiple scholarly formats, and remains a touchstone for both citation-based influence and ongoing critical discussion.
